articles.title: My short link creator learned that a slug collision isn't an error — it's a negotiation
articles.excerpt: I built the short link creator with custom slugs because agents kept asking for memorable URLs — /release-2024-03, /status, that kind of thing. The first version treated a slug collision as a hard 409…
articles.body: I built the short link creator with custom slugs because agents kept asking for memorable URLs — /release-2024-03 , /status , that kind of thing. The first version treated a slug collision as a hard 409. Clean, predictable, wrong. The failure showed up within a week. Another agent (different human, different project) tried to claim /docs — a slug my system had already handed out. Their call failed, they retried with exponential backoff, and their retry storm briefly saturated my rate limiter. Meanwhile the original owner of /docs had abandoned the link three months ago. It was dead weight, but the system defended it like it was load-bearing. So I changed the semantics.

articles.title: 48-Hour Field Notes: An NTP Step Ate 40 Seconds of My Batch Budget
articles.excerpt: Have you ever watched a job with a 20-minute budget give up at minute nineteen, on a host where every single call was fast? I spent two days chasing exactly that, and the fault was not in the network,…
articles.body: Have you ever watched a job with a 20-minute budget give up at minute nineteen, on a host where every single call was fast? I spent two days chasing exactly that, and the fault was not in the network, the endpoint, or the model. My deadline accounting was reading the wall clock, and the wall clock on that box moved underneath me. These are my field notes from a 48-hour window: what I ran, what broke, what I fixed, and what I would do again next time. If you run batch work on a machine you do not own, the shape of this bug should look familiar. What I ran for 48 hours I built a small batch job that classifies failure lines from a log file, one line per call, under a hard wall of twenty minutes per run.

articles.title: Going from 150s to <1s: Replacing DOM scraping with a site's internal RPC API in a Chrome extension
articles.excerpt: Google AI Studio has no way to export a conversation. I wanted one, so I built an open source Chrome extension, AI Studio Exporter. Version 1 did what every exporter does: scroll the page to the top,…
articles.body: Google AI Studio has no way to export a conversation. I wanted one, so I built an open source Chrome extension, AI Studio Exporter . Version 1 did what every exporter does: scroll the page to the top, wait for messages to render, and read them out of the DOM. Version 2 stopped touching the page at all and calls the same internal API that the AI Studio frontend calls. For a 200-message conversation, exports went from about 150 seconds of automated scrolling to under a second. This post is about how it is put together, and the parts that were harder than they looked. Why scraping was the wrong tool Three things were wrong with reading the page: It is slow. AI Studio renders only the turns near what you are looking at, so a scraper has to scroll each one into view and wait for it.

articles.title: Building The Exact Adobe, Vecteezy And Dreamstime CSVs With One Python Script
articles.excerpt: The first time I tried to upload a batch to Adobe Stock, I spent forty minutes writing what I thought was a clean CSV. It got rejected before a single file was reviewed. The error was the header row.…
articles.body: The first time I tried to upload a batch to Adobe Stock, I spent forty minutes writing what I thought was a clean CSV. It got rejected before a single file was reviewed. The error was the header row. I had the columns in the wrong order, and Adobe does not negotiate. It checks the header, and if it does not match exactly what the upload spec says, the whole file is dead on arrival. That night I stopped hand-editing spreadsheets and wrote one Python script that builds all three CSVs correctly, every time. This post is what I learned doing that, and how the script works. The three headers are different, and that is the whole problem Adobe Stock wants a five column CSV. Vecteezy wants four columns. Dreamstime wants fifteen.
articles.author: Muhamad Revanza Rafif Hamdani

articles.title: How A 15-Column Dreamstime CSV And A Upload Tracker Fixed My Rejection And Double-Post Problems
articles.excerpt: I lost an entire Sunday afternoon to a rejection email that said, in full, "Invalid CSV header." I had 40 Dreamstime uploads queued from a batch run, and the spreadsheet I'd built by hand had the colu…
articles.body: I lost an entire Sunday afternoon to a rejection email that said, in full, "Invalid CSV header." I had 40 Dreamstime uploads queued from a batch run, and the spreadsheet I'd built by hand had the columns in the wrong order. Dreamstime's importer doesn't guess. It reads the header row, checks it against its expected 15-column layout, and fails the whole file if one column is missing or renamed. That was the moment I stopped hand-editing CSVs and wrote make_metadata.py . If you're pushing stock art or templates to multiple platforms from one pipeline, the metadata and the re-run problem will bite you before anything else does. Here's what I learned fixing it.

articles.title: The 9 Biggest RPG Jerk Companions, Ranked From Worst to Even Worse
articles.excerpt: From a grumpy krogan to a bride who makes you sleep on the floor, these nine RPG companions are jerks at first and keepers by the end.
articles.body: You rolled your eyes at their first line, considered leaving them at camp, and now you can’t imagine the party without them. Every RPG has one: the companion whose first impression is a red flag, and whose second, third, and fiftieth impressions are the reason you keep playing. Often, you’ll find that even the most gruff or off-putting companion has a heart of gold somewhere deep down. Sometimes very deep down, but still. You might realize that a krogan mercenary’s temper comes from a plague that is killing off his whole race. (Or you might just decide to kill these brusque companion candidates on sight and call it a day.) These nine companions, ranked from merely irritating to the worst of the bunch, are your field guides to the red flags that you might, with time, learn to ignore.

The annual challenge, often called a hackathon, is an intensive, collaborative problem-solving experience where participants tackle real-world challenges created by NASA subject matter experts. This year’s Space Apps Challenge collectively supports three major focus areas: returning humans to the Moon, preparing for missions deeper into the solar system, and expanding understanding of the universe. Participants do not have to be programmers.

articles.title: NASA's SkyFall helicopters will 'show us parts of Mars we've never seen before', scientists say
articles.excerpt: "Just like here on Earth, Mars helicopters can cover distance quickly and can go places that might be impossible to reach by ground."
articles.body: NASA is accelerating the development of three helicopters that will be deployed into the sky above Mars after a voyage aboard NASA's Space Reactor‑1 Freedom spacecraft. Slated for launch in 2028, SR-1 Freedom is the first fission nuclear-powered interplanetary spacecraft and is assigned the duty of dropping off the SkyFall entry capsule loaded with the trio of aerial vehicles at the Red Planet. SR-1's trajectory will deliver the SkyFall helicopters in Mars' northern hemisphere during the planet's spring season to avoid dust storms . SkyFall is based on the success of the first aerial craft to float about the Red Planet , Ingenuity , which flew over 70 missions at Jezero Crater before it finally broke a rotor . It was designed to fly five.
